articles.title_zh: Dr Drew Pinsky reveals red flag in Presley Gerber addiction treatment before model's death
articles.content_orig:
When news broke that Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old son of Cindy Crawford, died Sunday at a California rehab facility, it raised questions about how someone with access to extensive treatment resources could still lose his life to addiction.
According to addiction specialist Dr. Drew Pinsky, Gerber’s case highlights the deadly, progressive nature of substance use disorder — and what he says is a dangerous trend in modern treatment: allowing patients to dictate their own care.
"When I listened to [Gerber's] video, what struck me and concerned me was that the patient seemed to be determining some of the care," Pinsky said on his podcast, "Ask Dr. Drew." "That's never good."
PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH SPARKS QUESTIONS ABOUT OVERDOSE, WITHDRAWAL AND REHAB SAFETY
Pinsky discussed Gerber’s self-reported trip to Mexico for an "ibogaine flood," referring to a high-dose treatment involving ibogaine, a psychoactive compound derived from an African shrub that has been studied as a potential treatment for substance use disorders but is not approved by the FDA.
"I've had patients using ibogaine or ayahuasca for decades, and there's nothing magic about it, I assure you," Pinsky warned, noting that almost every patient he’s seen try the alternative drug eventually relapsed on opioids, often suffering personality changes in the process.
Ibogaine remains an unapproved Schedule I substance in the U.S. due to documented risks of fatal heart arrhythmias, according to federal health agencies.
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
Pinsky argued that Gerber’s case highlights how patients struggling with severe substance use disorder are often allowed to bypass proven medical protocols in favor of risky alternative therapies.

Addressing public shock that the young model died inside a treatment center, Pinsky emphasized that high-end rehab centers cannot magically halt severe opioid dependence.
"Opioid addiction is progressive and it ends in death," Pinsky said. "Even with good treatment, it has a worse prognosis than most cancers ... If they are not moving toward recovery, they are moving toward demise."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While official toxicology results from the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office are still pending, emergency dispatch logs indicate that 911 was called to Gerber's facility for a suspected overdose and cardiac arrest.

Dr. Nicholas Kardaris, an addiction expert and CEO of the New York Center for Living, noted that the period inside or immediately following rehab is often the most dangerous window a patient faces.
"People are in rehab because they’re struggling with addiction. It doesn’t mean they’re cured," Kardaris told Fox News Digital, pointing out that when patients relapse in treatment, their lowered tolerance can turn their usual dose into a fatal one.

Medical experts maintain that families needing help for loved ones should seek evidence-based treatment from qualified providers, including FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorders, such as buprenorphine, methadone and naltrexone, when appropriate.

articles.title_orig: Hayden Panettiere died from an overdose involving fentanyl. She had just gone to rehab, coroner says
articles.title_zh: Hayden Panettiere died from an overdose involving fentanyl. She had just gone to rehab, coroner says
articles.content_orig:
Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose
Actress Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina.
The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death.
Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence.
The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse.
The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions.
Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone.
The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful".
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.
Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.
Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression.
Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy.
"I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without."
Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

articles.title_orig: Motorola Signature 27 Is Coming to the US to Rival Samsung’s Galaxy Phones
articles.title_zh: Motorola Signature 27 Is Coming to the US to Rival Samsung’s Galaxy Phones
articles.content_orig:
Just when we thought Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro would be the last major flagship phone to be released in 2026 in the US, Motorola decided to step in by debuting the Signature 27 on Tuesday, during Qualcomm’s annual Snapdragon Summit. Unlike the original Signature, this one will be coming to US markets, and it looks like an aggressive entry into the high-end Android flagship phone market.
Motorola’s Signature 27 will include the newly announced Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, coupled with a partial list of high-end features that remind me of the recently departed OnePlus phone line.
In addition to the early inclusion of Qualcomm’s chip, Motorola is touting a camera system that will include a 50-megapixel main camera along with a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto lens — the latter of which could be a boon for taking zoom photos from far distances, like at a concert. And there appear to be more cameras than Motorola has given details for, as the back of the phone shows four lenses, similar to Samsung’s quad-camera system on the Galaxy S26 Ultra.
For gamers — another audience that OnePlus had particularly focused on — the Signature 27 includes a cooling system that Motorola calls ArcticMesh. It combines a diamond-infused thermal gel, liquid metal, copper mesh and a 3D vapor chamber that’s 40% larger than the previous Signature phone — and should help it stay cool during intensive gaming and video recording.
The Signature 27 also matches Samsung’s Galaxy and Google’s Pixel lines with a seven-year commitment to software and security support, plus it will get an audio system developed in partnership with Bang & Olufsen. The Signature 27 is the first phone to get this audio system as part of a multiyear partnership with B&O, so it’s possible that down the road, the foldable Razr line will also benefit from this.
The Signature 27 will come in two colors with long names: “Pantone Coal Smoke in tactical weave” is a darker shade that features a woven texture for enhanced grip. “Pantone Capulet Olive in a brushed textile-inspired finish” is a green shade with a softer, tactile feel.
Motorola still has a lot of other details to unveil about the Signature 27, including its battery, charging speeds and display. But the first Signature phone the company debuted at CES 2026 in January included a 5,200-mAh silicon-carbon battery, 90-watt wired charging and a 6.8-inch display with a 165Hz refresh rate — all helpful reference points for what to expect in its successor. In Europe, the phone was priced at 999 euros (approximately $1,170 including tax) with 512GB of storage.
Even if the Signature 27 were to recycle some of its predecessor’s specs — and somehow hold onto its pricing despite rising costs brought on by the ongoing RAM shortage — on paper, this could be a tempting draw for former OnePlus phone fans looking for a new alternative as well as a tempting rival to Samsung’s next Galaxy phone.
We’ll find out more about the Motorola Signature 27 at a later date, with the phone set for release sometime before the end of the year.

articles.title_orig: Sri Lanka Convicts 15 in Easter 2019 Bomb Attacks
articles.title_zh: Sri Lanka Convicts 15 in Easter 2019 Bomb Attacks
articles.content_orig:
Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
Sri Lanka's High Court has given long jail sentences to 15 men charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.
Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.
The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.
All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.
The 15 defendants on Tuesday were each given prison terms ranging from 200 to 260 years.
The court in the capital Colombo also ordered the confiscation of their all movable and immovable assets.
The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the court in two prison buses.
Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children.
They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo.
The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans.
Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there.
In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.
In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.
Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.
For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.
The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.
The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.
Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.
Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

articles.title_orig: Ten Issues to Watch at the Trump-Xi Summit in Washington
articles.title_zh: Ten Issues to Watch at the Trump-Xi Summit in Washington
articles.content_orig:
Ten Issues to Watch at the Trump-Xi Summit in Washington
The honors for Xi exceed what Trump got in Beijing, but the asymmetry goes beyond the pageantry. A quick brief on ten issues that will define the state visit.
- Rush DoshiCFR ExpertC.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative
On Wednesday, President Xi Jinping lands at Joint Base Andrews for his first state visit to Washington in eleven years. President Donald Trump, in an unprecedented gesture, will be waiting for him on the tarmac. Later, a B-2 Spirit and four F-22 Raptors will overfly the ceremony, and Melania Trump will host Peng Liyuan, the first lady of China, for their own meeting. Nothing like this occurred when Trump visited Beijing in May of this year.
Although “reciprocity” is the Trump administration’s watchword for the summit and for China policy, the asymmetry in pageantry reveals something about an overall asymmetry in the relationship. Beijing believes it has tamed the Trump administration with rare earth export controls, and the Trump administration at times seems to believe it too. The Trump administration had retaliatory tools back in 2025 (from sanctions on smaller Chinese banks to export controls targeting a range of other chokepoints), but it opted not to use them and instead reduced tariffs in response to Beijing, culminating in the October “Busan deal.” Beijing’s ability to turn back U.S. tariffs marked an inflection point that established, as I wrote in The New York Times, China as a true peer of the United States, albeit one ahead on some metrics of power and behind on others.
The current “détente but not quite a détente” suits Beijing just fine. It believes the world is undergoing “great changes unseen in a century,” the foremost of which is the “rise of the east and decline of the west,” and that competition with the United States has entered a period of “strategic stalemate” as China gains in relative strength. It wants to use the next few years to consolidate its rise and reach what one might call escape velocity in its competition with Washington, using the calendar of leader meetings in November (Shenzhen) and December (Miami) to “manage” Washington. After that point, Washington’s leverage diminishes further. All the same, tensions are brewing.
Beijing wants to extend what it sees as Trump’s de-escalatory approach through the rest of his term. It has escalated in some cases: issuing new State Council directives that effectively criminalize decisions by firms to move production out of China, throttling supplies of rare earths despite the Busan deal, detaining U.S. citizens, and, reportedly, providing satellite imagery to Iran used in a strike that caused American fatalities. Washington has taken some steps of its own, including de facto bans on Chinese drones and robots, an advisory accusing Chinese firms of distilling American AI models, and a new law authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, China among them.
But the President favors stability, and the administration has taken far fewer such steps than many, including Beijing, expected. It has postponed a Section 301 finding that would raise tariffs on China, delayed a Taiwan arms package possibly until the end of the year, shrugged at China’s support for Iran, and kept tariff rates on China close to those on close allies.
In the background are two time-sensitive items: the expiration of the current tariff truce on November 10, and growing concern about AI risk.
The summit isn’t likely to produce many deliverables. Both sides want favorable optics. Trump faces midterms in under six weeks. Xi returns home to begin a year-long run-up to next fall’s Party Congress, where he is expected to secure another five-year term. At most, we will likely see a temporary extension of the Busan truce, some agricultural and energy purchases by China, and an AI dialogue.
Below, a quick summary of the state of play, issue by issue.
1. The Busan truce expires November 10, and Washington says Beijing hasn’t held up its end.
Beijing reportedly wants the truce extended through the end of Trump’s term, while U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said three to six months would be acceptable. The administration believes China hasn’t kept its side of the deal, telling the Financial Times that only two-thirds of its rare earth commitments have been fulfilled and that a shorter extension “serves as a compliance period for assessment.”
What this suggests is that the administration is reserving the right to again raise tariffs. Much depends, as officials put it, on whether Beijing’s rare earth throttling is “a glitch in the system” or “an intentional haircut.”
2. Washington is holding its tariff actions in reserve.
Washington has delayed a Section 301 report recommending a 7.5 percent tariff on China, which was part of an excess-capacity investigation launched in March involving 16 countries. Beijing says the Trump administration promised to cap “replacement” tariffs, imposed after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, at 20 percent. Washington hasn’t confirmed that.
Washington also has a new, unused lever. On September 18, Trump signed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which authorizes tariffs of up to 100 percent on the largest importers of Russian oil and gas, China among them, and extends the Iran Sanctions Act by five years.
3. Purchase commitments remain murky.
Something remarkable happened at the Beijing summit in May: Trump announced Chinese purchases of 200 Boeing aircraft and new agricultural commitments. Beijing, however, declined to confirm any of it. It is rare to see such misalignment over core deliverables hours after a summit.
Some progress on agricultural exports to China seems likely. Boeing aircraft, though, are probably being held hostage to disagreements over parts. Beijing doesn’t want Washington to have a chokepoint.
4. The Board of Trade is the likeliest vehicle for new deals.
For now, purchase commitments will probably flow through the still-nebulous “Board of Trade” announced in May. Greer says the Board is operational and that the two sides are drafting initial lists of products to trade. These likely include consumer and low-tech goods from China, and energy (such as LNG), farm goods, and medical devices from the United States. Some reports suggest tariff cuts on $30 billion in two-way trade, and Beijing might drop its tariffs on LNG.
5. A breakthrough on Chinese auto investment is unlikely.
Trump told Fox News he would be “OK” with Chinese automakers building plants in the United States if they employ Americans. The auto industry pushed back, arguing such investment would disproportionately benefit Chinese companies. American cabinet officials and unions, as well as Chinese regulators and automakers, have all been cool to the idea. A breakthrough seems unlikely, though a senior official told the Financial Times that the issue is not fully settled.
History suggests the need for some caution. In 2017, China promised $83.7 billion in investment in West Virginia. None of it materialized.
6. The AI dialogue moves forward. But questions linger.
Bessent, Greer, and He Lifeng agreed to an AI dialogue and possibly a new crisis communications line for AI. What will come of it is unclear. Bessent says the next meeting will likely be in two months, probably in Shenzhen. That is quite a gap.
I think four questions are outstanding:
- Are the right agencies at the table? Treasury and USTR negotiated this with He Lifeng, which is the right way to secure a summit deliverable but does not involve the agencies that deliver AI safety. Progress runs through NDRC, MOST, MIIT, the CAC, MOFCOM, and the MSS, and it is unclear whether they were in the room or will be.

China’s swimming prodigy Yu Zidi bags third gold in Asian Games record
The 13-year-old beat the previous 400m Asian Games record, set by China’s Ye Shiwen in 2014, by about 4.5 seconds.
China’s 13-year-old swimming sensation Yu Zidi has completed a hat-trick of Asian Games golds with a dominant victory in the 400m individual medley, two years before the Los Angeles Olympics.
The schoolgirl powered home in an Asian Games-record 4 minutes 28.56 seconds (04:28.56) on Wednesday to make it a clean sweep of her three individual events in Tokyo, following victories in the 200m butterfly and 200m individual medley, also in games-record times.

The story of her introduction to competitive swimming after being spotted by a coach at a water park, and her struggle with interviews, has gone viral on local social media platforms.

articles.title_orig: For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
articles.title_zh: For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
articles.content_orig:
For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
When Ziqiang Yuan moved to the U.S. in 1999, democracy was the last thing on her mind. Political speech was suppressed under socialist rule in her native China, and her aversion to politics stayed with her when she emigrated.
“We have a saying in China, ‘不谈政治.’ That means, ‘don't talk about politics,’ ” Yuan said. “You can get in trouble.”
Yuan, 55, goes by Susan now. She left Wuhan for the U.S. to pursue a post-doc in biomedical research, a field that then offered few opportunities in China while demand here was high. She even landed a scholarship.
But when her landlady brought Yuan to a local municipal meeting, eager to show the young grad student what American democracy looked like, something changed in Yuan. She was impressed that ordinary people were even aware of government gatherings, let alone that they could attend.
“That city council meeting really opened my eyes,” Yuan said. “You can have a chance to speak — directly speak — to those officials.”
Decades later, that first brush with local government would lead Yuan to try her chances at politics, a pathway she couldn’t have imagined had she stayed in China.
Yuan is among 175,000 people of Chinese descent who call Massachusetts home, including one in six Quincy residents. For most of U.S. history, Chinese immigrants have journeyed here in hopes of a better life. Their aspirations have varied decade to decade, and person to person. Indeed, ask people in Quincy about the American dream and the answers are as varied as the food options along Hancock and Beale streets.
Interviews with Chinese immigrants spanning multiple generations suggest the allure of the U.S. is being put to the test, amid a torrent of immigration restrictions under President Trump and the emergence of China as the world’s second-largest economy. But for many, the core draw of America remains strong, whether that’s for greater wealth, liberty or cultural freedoms that are elusive in China.
On a recent weekend in a downtown event space in Quincy, seniors in classical Chinese attire acted out the myth of the immortal moon goddess.
The Mid-Autumn Festival celebration was organized by Frank Poon of the nonprofit Civic Education Alliance. Poon came to the U.S. during a wave of Chinese immigration in the 1980s. Ronald Reagan was president, Beijing relaxed restrictions on its citizens’ ability to leave the country and the British would agree to transfer Hong Kong to Chinese control.
Poon said he knows success in the U.S. is far from guaranteed — and it often takes a lifetime of struggle.
“We’re still aiming at the American dream,” Poon said, and that people like him are “willing to invest all our time, all our effort, to make it come true.”
Looking back, Poon said he’s achieved what brought him to America 43 years ago. For him, that success has been more spiritual than something that can be measured.
“My American dream is, ‘I want to have a better life,’ ” he said. “I do have a better family. I do have opportunity to work with the community, and deep inside, in my heart and soul, I feel good.”
But one attendee of the harvest festival had something to say about a dream deferred.
In 1988, Carol Chu followed her future husband to Boston, with little money and no family here.
“The United States is such a freedom country,” she said. “I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely.”
Soon after they settled, however, Chu began to realize those things might be out of reach. She became pregnant, and her husband developed a severe gambling addiction. The worst part was when Chu lost custody of her son.
“I [was] so disappointed when I came here, because my American dream totally has not come true,” she said.
Instead of returning to her country, Chu stayed in the U.S. in order to be with her son, even if she could only see him one hour at a time.
"The United States is such a freedom country. I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely."
Chu recently retired after 37 years working for the Postal Service, and as the years have brought her closer to her son, she said she is finally happy here. Now that her boy is grown, Chu plans to split her time between China and the U.S.
“I think my duty is done,” she said.
Over the decades since these folks emigrated to the U.S., China has roared forward as an economic titan, with hundreds of millions emerging from extreme poverty. For the Chinese youth of today, that adds a new dimension to the decision to leave, whether for the U.S. or anywhere else in the world.
At Quincy’s Wollaston Beach, dozens of Chinese youth spread out on the sand, playing mahjong and practicing the Cantonese language. It was a meetup of the Boston Cantonese Club, and DJ Amanda Lou was spinning pop music under a tent.
The recent Boston University graduate is from Macau, a special administrative region of China ruled by the Portuguese until 1999. She spoke about the American ideal more in terms of culture than economic opportunities or political freedom. For her and many other Chinese graduates, Lou said, the exposure to freedom and different lifestyles is a strong motivation to stay.
“In Boston, I can just wear whatever I want, right? I can wear a tank top, shorts, walk outside — nothing will change," she said. "No one's going to stare at you."
At 23, Lou is ready to make a life in Boston. But remaining in the U.S. has never been a certainty for international students. It depends on factors like finding an employer to sponsor a visa petition. And with the current administration looking to add massive fees for foreign worker visas — and to favor “higher-skilled and higher-paid” applicants — big challenges loom for people like Lou.
“What happens if I don't find an employer who's willing to sponsor me?” she said. “Even if they do, what happens if I get fired or something? Definitely very stressful.”
Lou hopes to open a jazz bar in Boston one day, but if America is out of reach, she’ll have to bring her dreams elsewhere.
This kind of uncertainty is well-known to Vincent Lau, an immigration attorney in Boston. Much of his work involves helping American companies secure work visas. Lau said the traditional legal routes still exist, but they have increasingly narrowed under President Trump.
Among an array of measures to tighten rules on student immigration, Lau said consular officers now hold greater discretion to deny visa petitions, making it more difficult to advise parents on the wisdom of sending their kids to the U.S.
“Applying for the visas at the consulates has become much more challenging for Chinese citizens in general,” Lau said, “especially for students.”
On top of that, the administration is cutting research funding and suing elite universities, which Lau said have long been reliable paths to success in America. The administration has threatened to revoke visas for some Chinese students, and it accused Harvard of collaborating with the Chinese Communist Party.
Lau said the draw to study and live in the U.S. remains strong, but those policies are taking a toll.
“When [universities] are not being backed by the government, when they are being attacked by the government, it's not a quote-unquote, safe place,” Lau said. “It's not a place where people want to go.”
The impetus to immigrate has also changed as Chinese universities rise in global rankings. More Chinese youth are pursuing their studies in China. At the same time, an increasing number of students are returning home after graduating overseas.
But for Boston Cantonese Club organizer Alex Ng, China is no promised land. Ng said the Chinese tech economy suffers from a "race to the bottom" mentality, more driven by the search for rock bottom prices than by innovation. Ng said competition for jobs is fiercer in China than in the U.S., and that's especially hard for college grads.

articles.title_orig: At US-China summit, Trump should ask Xi to release my brother | Opinion
articles.title_zh: At US-China summit, Trump should ask Xi to release my brother | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
At US-China summit, Trump should ask Xi to release my brother | Opinion
My brother Ekpar Asat built a successful tech company, then vanished into a Chinese prison. I ask President Trump to raise his case at the White House summit with Xi Jinping.
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington this week, he is expected to bring a large delegation of Chinese business executives. The message is clear: Beijing wants America to see a China of entrepreneurship, innovation and economic opportunity that rivals the United States.
Before China made him a political prisoner, my brother Ekpar Asat embodied that promise.
In his 20s, Ekpar built Bagdax, a successful Uyghur-language multimedia technology platform in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. A prominent Chinese tech journal named him a rising star. He believed that China’s opening to the world had created possibilities unimaginable to the generation before him.
In 2016, at the invitation of the U.S. Embassy, Ekpar traveled to the United States to participate in the State Department’s premier International Visitor Leadership Program. He met with U.S. lawmakers, exchanged ideas with American institutions and was welcomed into American homes. Ekpar returned inspired by America’s institutions, its technology sector and the families who opened their homes to him.
My brother is caught between China and America
After Ekpar came home, Beijing detained him and said nothing. Nearly four years later, my family learned, through a Chinese Embassy response to a letter from U.S. lawmakers, that Ekpar had been sentenced to 15 years for "inciting ethnic hatred and ethnic discrimination." We have never seen a verdict, a trial record or any evidence.
The charge fails even by Beijing's own law, which caps that offense at 10 years and only in especially serious cases.
Nor does it fit the man. House Democrats noted in 2020 that Chinese media had portrayed Bagdax favorably, as a bridge across cultural divides.
The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found Ekpar's detention arbitrary. Republican and Democratic senators have said he was jailed for a "fabricated crime" and condemned his "opaque sentencing without a fair trial." The State Department says it has raised his case with Beijing, and Congress has noted he was detained days after taking part in the department’s exchange program.
In May, the Senate passed a resolution urging President Donald Trump to prioritize the release of my brother and others in his dealings with Xi.
For a decade, the world has come to know Ekpar as a political prisoner. I knew him long before that label existed – as the best brother a sister could hope for. His colleagues knew a restless entrepreneur. Young people across the Uyghur homeland knew the platform he had built. Families knew him for helping children with disabilities and others in need. Prison did not make Ekpar significant. It interrupted a life in motion.
Ekpar began building Bagdax fresh out of college. While many of his classmates sought the security of conventional jobs, he wanted to build something new. My parents were skeptical. I wasn’t. Whenever Ekpar talked about Bagdax, he lit up. I persuaded them to let him choose his own path.
They eventually agreed, on one condition: They would provide no financial support. Ekpar started anyway. His apartment had bare cement walls, unfinished and unpainted – the first thing visitors noticed when they walked through the door. There was barely any furniture beyond a bed and a small kitchen. From that apartment, armed with his computer-science training, imagination and sheer persistence, he built Bagdax brick by brick.
What Beijing's pitch to Washington leaves out
That is what makes Ekpar's imprisonment more than a harrowing injustice. His story also exposes the contradiction at the heart of the economic confidence Beijing now wants to project abroad. China took a man doing precisely what governments everywhere say they want young people to do: create, innovate, build a business, serve a community, travel abroad, learn and come home.
When Xi comes to Washington, he will ask American businesses to have confidence in China. But Ekpar’s story exposes a contradiction in that pitch: What protection does business success offer when political power can still erase an entrepreneur’s freedom, business and future?
Beijing’s hypocrisy extends beyond trade. It promotes people-to-people exchange between the United States and China, yet Ekpar remains imprisoned after participating in a U.S. government exchange program.
Xi has long urged Chinese officials to tell China’s stories well, to present a China that is credible and appealing to the outside world. During his visit, President Trump should ask him about another China story: Ekpar’s. He should raise Ekpar’s case directly and ask for my brother's release.
For Xi, the test is just as straightforward. If Beijing wants Americans to believe that China is a country where entrepreneurs can build and prosper, and that Americans and Chinese can engage safely through the people-to-people exchanges both governments have long promoted, there is a simple way to demonstrate it.
Let one of those entrepreneurs, an alumnus of a U.S. government exchange program, walk free.
Rayhan Asat is a human rights lawyer and scholar. She serves as a senior legal and policy adviser and China project lead at the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project.

articles.title_orig: Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
articles.title_zh: Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
The Chinese leader has to deal with a legitimacy crisis at home. The U.S. leader knows that Republicans' success in the midterm elections depend on economic relief for the American people, fast.
A leadership summit between any two countries is always cause for pressure-packed preparations by all relevant agencies, but for the Sept. 24 White House U.S.-China summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the stakes have arguably never been higher.
China faces the loss of 18 million factory jobs, rampant income inequality and a 70% increase in rural protests between 2024 and 2025.
The United States faces skyrocketing oil prices, persistent threats of escalation from Iran and China’s alarming trade surplus.
For big "bilaterals" like this one set for Thursday, every Cabinet agency and all senior White House staff scurry to put together an agenda. Here are strategies they'll likely submit to the president as bases for memorandums of understanding, which will come from the meetings if executed well.
Trump, Xi should call for a world conference on AI
Trump and Xi, first and foremost, could agree to participate in and lead a world conference on artificial intelligence, with positive usages and safeguards.
Trump must seek a halt to China’s rampant intellectual property theft, which has enabled Chinese companies to save billions of dollars training their AI on American frontier models.
However, because both countries deeply mistrust the other to fairly navigate AI safety on their own, the leaders must address patent and copyright theft laws, and implement AI guardrails against human harm. Offered in a spirit of friendly competitors, this could benefit both countries and the world.
A joint statement could be significant.
Gain more rare earth metals for the United States
In 2025, Beijing began requiring foreign companies to obtain a special government-approved license to ship certain products containing rare earth metals sourced from China.
To obtain these licenses, companies had to share highly sensitive data, including profiles of end-users.
Companies affiliated with foreign militaries would be largely denied licenses unless Washington maintains some information access (now recognizing U.S. military’s dependence on Chinese rare earth elements) but the United States and China could agree on mutual assistance.
There could be higher tariffs or tighter restrictions on China’s access to semiconductors unless China withdraws its expanded license requirements.
Clarify US-China research collaboration
Recently, millions of dollars of Washington funding for colleges has helped Beijing develop critical military technology through academic research involving organizations affiliated with China’s defense industrial base, according to a House Republican report.
In response, clarify and regulate more strongly research collaboration between American universities and Chinese-military-affiliated organizations.
Negotiate guardrails on tech components that can spy
Mounting evidence reveals that Chinese tech components can secretly transmit information to China.
This is a massive national security risk, particularly due to the U.S. military’s reliance on Chinese batteries. Trump must secure restrictions on components sold to the United States with surveillance capabilities.
Maintain strategic ambiguity on Taiwan
Taiwan remains the strictest red line for China, so any diplomatic negotiation requires strategic ambiguity on Taiwan contingencies. Remain vague about whether the United States would militarily support Taiwan in the case of a Chinese invasion.
Keep the $14 billion pending Taiwan arms sale up for negotiation and leave for later after this summit, depending on Xi’s openness to other demands, and signal support for China while keeping future options open to support Taiwan if necessary.
Pledge to reduce oil prices
Washington wants Beijing to buy American goods. Unfortunately, rising oil prices from the Iran war exacerbated production costs in China, slowing down its economic growth, and driving the Chinese to buy fewer American goods.
Trump could pledge de-escalation attempts with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to bring down oil prices. Clarify that China should stop buying Iranian oil until the Strait of Hormuz is opened, and that China should expand its agreement to import more American agricultural goods.
Cooperate on drug policy, target methamphetamine and fentanyl
Expand the McCaffrey-China anti-drug agreement made more than a quarter-century ago on methamphetamine and now fentanyl.
In 2000, retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, as head of the Office of National Drug Control Policy, led a delegation to China and negotiated a drug treatment and source prevention agreement. He explained that for China itself, treatment was more than warehousing thousands of addicts cold turkey in a big room in a Chinese city. It meant stop allowing import of drugs from Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, and providing jobs and counseling for addicts.
Now, China is a major source of devastating fentanyl in the United States. An agreement to help each other could be a productive component of the Trump-Xi summit.
To solidify long-term trust, Trump should increase cultural ties between the two nations by renewing a commitment to sharing arts and sports – like Chinese table tennis and U.S. football diplomacy – and inviting China’s National Peking Opera back to the United States.
Both Trump and Xi are at a crossroads
Xi faces a legitimacy crisis. While many of his citizens have long supported the Chinese Communist Party’s overall economic prosperity, China’s stagnating economy and skyrocketing youth unemployment have greatly weakened the party's internal political legitimacy.
For his part, Trump’s reversing his low approval ratings ahead of the November midterm elections (and, consequently, the Republican Party’s success) depends on his ability to deliver economic relief, and fast. That can be accomplished by increasing American exports to China.
Chinese leaders are as interested in making productive deals with the United States as we are with them, making the Trump-Xi summit an enormous opportunity for the two global superpowers as well as the world.
Robert Weiner was a spokesman in the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations, the White House drug policy spokesman, chief of staff for the House Aging Committee, and communications director of the House Government Operations and Oversight Committee. Emmbrooke Flather is a senior policy analyst at Robert Weiner Associates, and served as copresident of the Chinese Culture Club at Phillips Academy Andover. At Boston College, she studied Mandarin, East Asian Security and the Rise of China.

articles.title_orig: China's new travel curbs to prevent key talent from leaving unsettles tech firms and workers
articles.title_zh: China's new travel curbs to prevent key talent from leaving unsettles tech firms and workers
articles.content_orig:
China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
For decades, China has faced accusations from the United States and the European Union of stealing their technology.
From robotics and advanced semiconductors to precision engineering and automotive parts, Chinese firms have recruited top engineers, allegedly spied on Western rivals and been linked to cyberattacks aimed at gaining access to valuable trade secrets.
It is perhaps ironic, then, that China is now taking steps to prevent its own high-end technologies and talent from escaping abroad.
China's Great Wall around its top brains
Last week, new entry-exit rules took effect, giving Chinese authorities the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI) is judged a threat to "industrial and technological security."
Recently, China has also tightened outbound-investment rules, cracked down on Chinese nationals holding their wealth offshore and restricted the posting of technical staff overseas.
Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University (SMU), believes that, taken together, the curbs "offer a rare glimpse into the true state of China's economy."
"These measures suggest that Beijing is deeply concerned about economic weakness and substantial capital outflows," Gao told DW, adding that authorities are also determined to stop "entrepreneurs and skilled personnel from leaving the country."
The strain on China's economy is increasingly hard to hide. While demand for exports remains strong — especially for high-tech goods — the country's property crash has severely weakened domestic consumption.
Bank lending fell to a record low over the summer, and new car sales in August dropped nearly a quarter year-on-year.
Beijing blocks deals, founders seek exit
The same anxiety now extends to people and money leaving. The most prominent recent example is Manus, an AI startup created by two Chinese nationals in Beijing. Last year, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore, partly to avoid US investment curbs and expand into global markets.
When Facebook owner Meta tried to acquire Manus last December for $2 billion (€1.74 billion), Beijing blocked the move and barred the firm's two founders from leaving the country.
Just this month, Chinese social media has been awash with rumors that Huawei founder and CEO Ren Zhengfei and his daughter, CFO Meng Wanzhou, may have left the country.
The claims were picked up by Taiwanese and Indian media outlets but have not been confirmed by the tech giant and Chinese authorities. At least one family member has since appeared in public in Beijing.
Wealthy Chinese struggle to get capital out
Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that some $1 trillion in Chinese wealth had exited the country last year — the largest amount of "hot money" leaving since 2006, when records began.
Beijing has not tightened its annual $50,000 foreign-exchange quota that households may take out of the country. What has tightened, says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis, are the unofficial routes the wealthy used around that cap.
"They haven't changed the $50,000 quota. They are now squeezing the people and agents that money usually travels with," Garcia-Herrero told DW.
An entire industry has grown up, in China and abroad, to help people get themselves and their capital out. Emigration agents arrange visas and relocations, while offshore brokers and trusts help Chinese nationals to park wealth overseas.
Companies sometimes use a foreign subsidiary, a listing or a staff posting to take money and know-how out together.
New rules may spur workarounds
SMU's Gao believes the new curbs may prove counterproductive, as the more difficult it becomes to move capital or people abroad, the greater the incentive for those with the means to find other ways out.
"Over time, that could further erode confidence, accelerate capital flight and deepen the very economic problems the measures are intended to contain," Gao told DW.
Garcia-Herrero, meanwhile, thinks the block on talent will matter more than the squeeze on capital.
"You can still move money slowly, with approvals," she told DW. "You cannot easily replace a process engineer who cannot board a plane — or who will not take an overseas job because of an indefinite ban."
AI talent now needs permission to fly
The risk is already hitting China's AI firms, which are fast catching up with their US rivals in the race to produce the most advanced AI systems.
In May, Bloomberg reported that Chinese authorities now required top AI researchers, founders and executives at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to obtain approval before traveling abroad.
Last year, some DeepSeek staff were asked to hand in their passports, according to tech news site The Information. Beijing has neither confirmed nor denied the practice.
Bloomberg reported in January last year that other tech engineers face similar pressure, including those helping foreign firms cut their reliance on China by building factories in Vietnam and India.
Lawyers and officials tighten legal advice
For foreign nationals, both Chinese and foreign firms sometimes disguise a working visit to China to avoid scrutiny and visa delays. They may suggest a trip is for tourism, business meetings or a factory tour rather than actual work.
Ahead of the new curbs, international law firms like DLA Piper advised companies to keep visa filings "truthful" and "complete," warning that a mismatch between the paperwork and the actual work could now mean an entry ban of up to five years.
The new rules state that a visitor should, in principle, be told if they are banned. However, Chinese authorities may withhold notification if it "may affect national security or the investigation of criminal cases."
In an updated travel advisory earlier this month, the US State Department went further, warning Americans to "exercise increased caution in mainland China due to ... the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

articles.title_orig: Soybeans, planes and rare earths: What they say about fragile U.S.-China trade truce
articles.title_zh: Soybeans, planes and rare earths: What they say about fragile U.S.-China trade truce
articles.content_orig:
Soybean purchases, orders for Boeing aircraft and access to rare earths elements — three of the headline commitments underpinning the U.S.-China trade truce — are progressing at markedly different speeds ahead of the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday.
Taken together, the uneven fulfillment record suggests the truce is performing its minimal function of keeping commerce moving and discouraging renewed escalation, but there is little willingness on either side to cede strategic leverage, analysts said.
"The truce is moving fastest where it costs least," Eric Xiao, head of sales for Asia at CMC Markets, told CNBC.
The superpowers' May meeting reaffirmed Beijing's commitment to increase purchases of U.S. soybeans and buy 200 Boeing aircraft, while Chinese shipments of rare earths magnets are back underway after export controls were suspended for a 12-month period beginning last November.
But delivery across the three commitments has been uneven, and difficult to verify in some cases.
Larry Hu, head of China economics at Macquarie Group, described the recent U.S.-China relationship as a phase of détente — a cooling of tensions — driven by "a balance of vulnerability."
Both sides are "acutely aware of the other's choke points," Hu said in a note.
The détente should not be mistaken for a rapprochement, according to Wendy Cutler, vice president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
"Each side has an interest in stability right now," Cutler told CNBC's "The China Connection" in May. "This doesn't mean we're going to become best friends, but it means we're going to coexist."
Soybeans: most visible lever
Soybeans offer the clearest numerical signal of progress across the trade commitments.
China has bought almost half its 25 million ton annual commitment after it purchased roughly one million tons from U.S. producers in a single week in September, Reuters reported.
Soybean purchases are also an important tool for signaling cooperation between the two nations.
"Things pick up a little bit before the bilateral meetings between Trump and Xi ... and then fall off again," China strategist Andy Rothman told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" in July, noting that purchases tended to cluster around key meetings.
Xiao described soybean purchases as "political trophies", but cautioned against interpreting soybean fulfillment as a direct sign of Beijing's stance on broader trade ties. "China buys them because it needs them," he said.
Soybean trade tiffs are not a recent development.
China, the world's largest soybean importer, saw U.S. soybeans plummet from 40% of total imports before Trump imposed tariffs on major Chinese goods in 2018, to 23% in the first five months of 2026.
Aircraft: slower, stickier pledge
Progress on the 200-aircraft commitment is less transparent.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer this week said roughly 140 aircraft were in a "good state," with orders for another 10 being written, according to Reuters. Customers, models and delivery timelines have not been disclosed.
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg has also downplayed expectations for a single 200-aircraft announcement, saying individual Chinese airlines would place and announce orders at their own pace.
The pledge came with additional caveats, with Beijing's official account of the May agreement tying the purchases to U.S. guarantees over the supply of aircraft engines and parts.
Rare earths: strategic leverage remains
Beijing's fulfillment of the rare earths commitment is harder to measure, because the promise concerns reliable access rather than a specified export volume.
Chinese shipments of rare earths magnets to the U.S. recovered after earlier restrictions, but fell to 512 metric tons in August — down 20% from July and 13% from a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data reported by the Financial Times.
Uncertainty around rare earths access also persists for U.S. customers.
Some Chinese suppliers have declined U.S. orders because of geopolitical and compliance concerns, while some American companies have waited more than six months for export licenses, Reuters reported.
Rare earths' strategic importance may provide the clearest signal of each nation's stance on trade ties because of the strategic cost of making concessions over the materials, experts said.
Macquarie's Hu identified rare earths as the principal Chinese choke point, balanced against U.S. leverage in advanced semiconductors used in chipmaking.
Xiao similarly called rare earths the clearest indicator of the broader relationship, due to their importance in clean energy, advanced technology and defense.
Progression on the rare earths commitment could "anchor a durable relationship in a way that soybean and aircraft orders cannot," Xiao said.
He noted that exercising that leverage is a delicate calculation. A complete cutoff of exports would encourage the U.S. and its allies to accelerate alternative supply chains while hurting Chinese producers that depend on global electric vehicle and technology markets.
China's "strongest card, in other words, is one it cannot play in full," Xiao said.

articles.content_orig:
China's Great Green Wall pushes back Gobi sands, and the scale is hard to grasp
A sweeping video gave viewers a striking look at one of the world's most ambitious restoration efforts. China's Great Green Wall is an ambitious program to hold back desert sands in Inner Mongolia.
Shared by the South China Morning Post (@scmp.news), the clip shows a long strip of greenery meeting the edge of the Gobi, with the vegetation holding the sand at bay.
"China's Great Green Wall stands against the spread of desert sands," the caption stated.
Desertification can swallow productive land, worsen dust storms, strain water resources, and make life harder for people living near vulnerable drylands.
"The goal is to prevent the spread of desertification from affecting the country's interior," Zhao Zhong, founder of Green Camel Bell, told SCMP. "So far the most visible part of this effort is large-scale afforestation."
When restoration succeeds at scale, the benefits can be significant. Efforts can protect homes, roads, farms, and local economies from mounting land loss.
"This is what long-term environmental restoration looks like," a commenter wrote. "Seeing the greenery return is remarkable. Imagine what another few decades of careful restoration could accomplish."
China's Great Green Wall is a long-term effort to slow the advance of desert landscapes by planting trees and other vegetation across vulnerable northern regions.
SCMP said the program used the "straw checkerboards" planting technique to help nearby greenery by kickstarting an irrigation system. It also stabilizes sand dunes against strong winds.
In practical terms, such projects are meant to anchor soil, reduce erosion, and create buffers that limit how easily sand moves into settled or cultivated areas.
When land degradation spreads, it can lower agricultural productivity, reduce air quality, and stress infrastructure with blowing sand and dust. Reversing those trends can support public health, food security, and economic stability.
"It has replaced desertification with a slowly expanding wall of green in communities across half of China," SCMP noted in the video.
Desert control depends on investment, maintenance, and land management over decades.
SCMP reported that the initiative has reduced desert spread by nearly 400 miles a year since 2000 and created forests spanning almost 200,000 square miles.
If vegetation reduces erosion and buffers settlements from sand encroachment, people living nearby may benefit from cleaner air, more stable land, and stronger local resilience. In the video, locals touted the progress of the initiative.
Zhu Jiaojun of the Chinese Academy of Science warned that consolidating the gains of the initiative might be the real test.
"Given such high levels of investment and such massive input, once it stops, can what we achieved be sustained?" he said.
SCMP concluded by saying local green groups are educating new farmers and herders on the importance of preventing desertification.
China is engaging in a number of large-scale efforts to fight desertification in the country.
• Officials completed a shelterbelt 46 years in the making around the Taklimakan Desert.
• Authorities used a revolutionary strategy to turn barren land into wetlands.
• Along the Great Wall of China, biocrusts shield weak points from further erosion.

articles.content_orig: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-and-ukraine-trade-strikes-ahead-of-zelenskyys-meeting-with-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia and Ukraine trade strikes ahead of Zelenskyy's meeting with Trump World Updated on Sep 22, 2026 6:09 PM EDT — Published on Sep 22, 2026 3:02 PM EDT UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Tuesday with his U.S. counterpart, Donald Trump and said he trusted that the White House can help end Russia's 4½-year war on his country — even as attacks from both sides keep escalating. "I hope that we will end this war, and President Trump will help us help us end this war," Zelenskyy said, joining Trump at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, where the Ukrainian president was meeting with world leaders. WATCH: NATO jets shoot down drone in Lithuania as Russia continues to provoke Europe That meeting occurred after Russian missiles and drones struck at least four Ukrainian regions overnight, strikes that officials said killed five people. Zelenskyy also said that his country's forces had damaged two more Russian oil refineries in their latest long-range strikes. The continuing exchange of aerial attacks, even as front-line positions remain largely unchanged. Trump previously had called on Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are contributing to global shortages and higher prices. The supply crunch has also been aggravated by reduced oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz following the outbreak of the Iran war. Trump and Zelenskyy briefly addressed reporters before heading behind closed doors. The U.S. president was asked about the Ukrainian strikes and called them "a serious hit on the Russians, but also a serious hit on the price of diesel" which he noted had "gone up quite a bit." Trump added that he and Zelenskyy would further discuss the matter privately. While seeking reelection in 2024, Trump once argued that he could in virtually no time broker an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, which instead has carried on. Russia invaded Ukraine more than 4½ years ago. Still, Trump said Tuesday, "I think we're going to make a deal" to quell the fighting. "We talked about it a lot, including with President Putin," Trump said of a possible agreement, meaning Russian leader Vladmir Putin. "And I think something's going to happen." Putin is not scheduled to attend the annual U.N. General Assembly meeting this year. Asked about the possibility of Zelenskyy, Putin and Trump meeting during the upcoming G20 gathering in Florida in December, Trump was noncommittal. In subsequent, solo comments to reporters, Zelenskyy said he was ready to sit down with both leaders but suggested that Putin might balk because he's not really ready to end the war. He also noted that Ukraine has continued to push the U.S. for more Patriot air defense systems in its efforts to defend itself, but has yet to get clear answers. "They are positive to help us, but I didn't get the very concrete answer," Zelenskyy said. Defense experts say the U.S. has been experiencing a global shortage of Patriot interceptors because many have been expended to defend against Iranian attacks on U.S. and allied bases in Middle East. Zelenskyy was also asked about the risk of offensive attacks by drones, missiles or land operations ordered by Moscow that could be high against other countries that border Russia or Belarus. He said such neighboring countries should "respond — always respond" to defend themselves. "If you don't respond," he added, "Russians, they will go further." Zelenskyy says Ukraine may end strikes if Russia makes concessions Kyiv began targeting Russian refineries after Moscow repeatedly attacked Ukraine's power grid. Zelenskyy says his country could halt them should Russia end its attacks on energy infrastructure. The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions. Western analysts estimate that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies. Russia and Ukraine have in recent years accounted for around 30% of the world's wheat exports and 12% of corn exports, most of it shipped through the Black Sea. But last month, attacks slashed both countries' agricultural exports by two-thirds, Thomas de Waal of the Brussels-based think tank Carnegie Europe said in a report Tuesday. "The lack of that grain in world markets puts several African countries at risk of famine, while world cereal prices, already pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, could rise even higher," de Waal said. Zelenskyy takes de-escalation proposals to New York French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that France would provide Ukraine with additional radar systems to help protect its power grid. Macron said in a social media post that he had discussed with Trump a possible truce between Moscow and Kyiv that would halt strikes on energy infrastructure, as well as a "moratorium" on attacks in the Black Sea. Zelenskyy began his visit to New York by meeting with U.S. senators. He thanked them for what he described as strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for backing a tougher sanctions bill against Russia that Trump signed into law. Peace and security would be closer once the legislation was fully implemented, Zelenskyy said. He said on social media that he had briefed senators on de-escalation proposals he was discussing privately with Trump. In Kyiv, Iryna Panina awoke around 2 a.m. on Tuesday as a jet-powered Russian drone approached her home. The blast shattered a window and left her apartment covered in debris. Panina, 36, said she had lost hope in international efforts to secure peace. "As an ordinary person just trying to live and survive each day, I find it hard to believe they fully understand what's actually happening, how hard it is, and how much ordinary people are suffering," she told The Associated Press. Ukraine hits a Russian oil refinery Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian special forces struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, and another refinery in the neighboring Bashkortostan region in overnight attacks. One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities," but didn't specify which ones. READ MORE: Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia, including 'largest ever' attack on Moscow The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula. Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said. The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration. A drone also killed a woman in the northern Sumy region, local police said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine. Barry Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal and Hanna Arhirova from Kyiv. articles.title_orig: Egypt, China unearth wine press at temple to ancient goddess
articles.title_zh: Egypt, China unearth wine press at temple to ancient goddess
articles.content_orig:
A limestone structure believed to have once served as a wine press was recently unearthed at the Temple of Sekhmet site near the village of Mit Rahina, the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced earlier this month.
Mit Rahina is located near the ancient ruins of Memphis, which in antiquity had served as the capital of the first nome of Lower Egypt.
In ancient Egyptian mythology, Sekhemet is considered both a warrior goddess and a goddess of medicine. Her temple makes up one part of the Great Temple of Ptah complex, which served as the main temple of ancient Memphis.
Discovered by a joint Egyptian-Chinese archaeological mission, the wine press includes an upper basin sloping downward toward a central opening and a lower collection basin, each topped with an opening designed to hold amphorae.
Archaeologists found grape seeds inside the press, supporting the archaeologists’ interpretation.
Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that the mission began its work by cleaning and documenting the Temple of Sekhmet as part of its excavations to understand how the site was used throughout the ages.
Mudbrick residential complex also unearthed
Additionally, the mission found the remains of a mudbrick residential complex in the area surrounding the temple, along with a series of stone blocks and statue fragments believed to have been part of Ptah’s temple.
Most of the blocks and fragments date back to the New Kingdom period, mainly during the reign of King Ramesses II, and are made from various types of stone, including limestone, red granite, and schist
Other artifacts found at the site include pottery shards, faience amulets, small terracotta and limestone statuettes, ostraca, and votive stelae.
Mohamed Abdel-Badie, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector at the Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that these discoveries indicate that there had been continuous human settlement in the area between the Third Intermediate Period and the Late Period, through the Ptolemaic era and up to the Greco-Roman period.
Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy expressed his pleasure at the collaboration between Egypt and China, two of the oldest civilizations in history.
The Temple of Sekhmet was discovered by chance in 1959, during the construction of a house in the area. Following this, Egyptian antiquities inspector Mohamed Abdel Tawab El-Hetta carried out a single season of excavations at the site from 1961 to 1962.
In 2015, the visible remains of the temple were documented as part of the Ancient Memphis Site and Community Management Project.
Deity-inscribed tombstones, sarcophagi unearthed at ancient Egyptian burial site
Earlier this summer, some 20 limestone tombstones, several sarcophagi, and a collection of funerary amulets were discovered during excavations at the Tell El Deir archaeological site.
The sides and backs of the tombstones are decorated with religious symbols and godly imagery, including that of a griffin, Agathodaemon, and Isis-Thermouthis.
Agathodaemon is a lesser serpent demon in ancient Graeco-Egyptian religion, as well as in classical Greek mythology. Isis-Thermouthis is a combination of the Egyptian goddess Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris, and Renenutet (Thermuthis), the Egyptian goddess of grain.
The appearance of the two deities on the tombstones points to joint Greek and Roman influence on ancient Egyptian heritage and funerary practices.
Further, the decorations allow archaeologists to identify the social status of the tombstones’ owners.
Additionally, the Egyptian archaeological mission operating at the site uncovered a collection of pottery incense burners, decorated lamps, and funerary amulets, as well as several barrel-shaped anthropoid ceramic coffins.

articles.title_orig: Nolan Wells’ family vows to ‘never stop’ seeking the truth after grand jury report
articles.title_zh: Nolan Wells’ family vows to ‘never stop’ seeking the truth after grand jury report
articles.content_orig:
Nolan Wells’ parents and their attorneys called on Mississippi to continue pursuing a fuller picture of the “truth” in the teenager’s death at a news conference Tuesday.
The news conference was held a day after the Jackson County district attorney said a state grand jury will not pursue charges in the teenager’s July Fourth death.
“Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McArthur will have you accept that Nolan Wells’ death can be summarized in three words: ‘We’ll never know,’” attorney Ben Crump said. “But Nolan’s family offers three other words: ‘We’ll never stop.’”
Crump, in his remarks, insinuated that the district attorney’s investigation was not exhaustive and should continue until the cause of Wells’ death is made clear.
Wells’ mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said she received a text message from the district attorney at 7:54 p.m. Monday, and that the report was released shortly after.
“To me, that action shows a lack of empathy,” she said.
Wells-Wonsley continued: “What we have learned is that we still have no answers, and the report reinforced the fact that Nolan was not given a thorough, transparent and honest investigation.”
The DA’s office shared the text with NBC News. It alerts Wells-Wonsley to the grand jury report, without revealing its conclusions. The DA offers to send it to Wells-Wonsley and offers to “support you in your grief.”
Wells, 18, was last seen celebrating the July 4 holiday with friends on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. The friends he was with that day have said they had to leave the island early because their boat was taking on water, and that Wells opted to stay behind for the rest of the day and told them he’d catch a ride back to the mainland with others.
His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, Crump has said.
In the aftermath of Wells’ death, Crump pointed the blame toward the friends Wells was with on that day, all of whom are white, and alleged that race played a role. Wells appeared to be one of the few Black people on the island that day, according to photos and videos shared of the celebrations.
District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath attempted to put that idea to rest with Tuesday’s statement.
In a video message, she said the grand jury did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime.
“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”
In an interview with NBC News, Wells-Wonsley said that “at no point in time have we ever made this a racial thing” but that “Unfortunately, the optics of the situation has kind of allowed a segue to that.”
She said that she and her husband, Elmore Wonsley, have only wanted to find out what happened to their son.
“I have always told our children, ‘I will move heaven and earth if anything were to ever happen,’ and that’s exactly what Elmore and I are doing,” she said.
Myers McIlrath took aim at Crump and his team on Monday, saying they’d previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.
Speaking with NBC News on Tuesday, Crump said he did not want to engage in a “tit for tat” with the DA and her office.
“The issue is about what happened to Nolan Wells,” he said. “Everything else is just a distraction.”
The Rev. Al Sharpton, who has been an advocate for the family, said skepticism is warranted from Wells’ parents and those following the case.
“Mississippi’s history painfully teaches us exactly why families should never be expected to simply accept unanswered questions surrounding the death of a young Black person,” the civil rights advocate said in a statement Tuesday.
Crump, along with Wells’ parents, commissioned an independent autopsy, which found the cause of the teenager’s death was “undetermined.” It did, however, find two bruises on the back of Wells’ head.
“To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” Crump said in a statement. “We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the state of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating.”
Crump and Wells-Wonsley both spoke about the apparent blunt force trauma again Tuesday at the news conference and called for answers.
The grand jury’s report, a partially redacted copy of of which was posted to the DA’s Facebook page, noted the bruising to the back of Wells’ head but concluded that it was “not a fatal injury.” A witness, it said, testified to seeing Wells awkwardly off the boat. The witness couldn’t tell if Wells hit his head but said he continued to socialize, the report stated.
Crump also called on the district attorney to release the full autopsy report from the medical examiner’s office.
Coroner Bruce Lynd said he will not be releasing the state’s autopsy report, telling NBC News the report, “which may include a toxicology report, cannot be released because the release of autopsy reports” is limited by Mississippi law.
The grand jury concluded that there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”
Crump and Wells’ parents have previously rejected the idea that he simply drowned, citing the teenager’s athleticism and ability to swim. Those who know the area well, though, told NBC News it is not uncommon for even a good swimmer to be swept away by the currents.
The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.
Crump said there will be another press conference in Orlando, Florida, later this week to discuss the investigation into Wells’ cellphone. The friends on the boat had his phone and brought it back to the mainland from Horn Island on July 4.
